attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post, written in his voice.

semantics.note: The drafter keeps 'it appears', 'at present' and both scopes. But 'it appears' marks the whole sentence as tentative, including the disclosure clause. This is a graded-confidence generalisation, not a firm assertion.

contract.note: The contract applies a plain reading and sets support conditions as if the statement were firm. Policy does not allow a plain reading of hedged language. It also adds its own population, snapshot date and 'how much' test, none of which the speaker gave.

evidence.note: Waymo's own March 2023 safety paper, published before the post. It describes remote assistance but gives no numbers on how much it contributes to results. It cannot settle the industry-majority claim or the disclosure claim.

reviews.rationale: The claim is introduced with 'It appears', so it is a tentative generalisation and is not scored under policy. Even if it were scored, the only item is a single company's disclosure. It establishes neither an industry-wide denominator nor whether any published figure quantified remote assistance's contribution, so the result would be unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post. The point about other companies is his own report of rumours.

semantics.note: The firm assertion is about Cruise. The rumour qualifier on other companies is kept. The proposition leaves out 'the car does some of the work', but the scored core, frequent calls to a remote centre, is intact.

contract.note: Reading 'frequently' as a routine, recurring part of operations, not continuous control, is an ordinary plain reading. Limiting the scored part to Cruise matches the qualifier on the others.

evidence.note: CNBC report, with comments the company confirmed: remote assistance 2-4% of the time and requests about every 4-5 miles before the October 2023 pause. This shows recurring calls. It is a company disclosure, which the contract accepts, and advisors gave guidance rather than driving remotely.

reviews.rationale: Cruise confirmed that its driverless cars requested remote assistance roughly every 4-5 miles, about 2-4% of the time, before the October 2023 pause. That is routine, frequent calling, so the firm claim about Cruise holds. The evidence does not show remote driving, which the claim did not assert. The rumour about other companies is not scored.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The universal antecedent ('all', 'hourly' example) is kept, and no deadline is given. The 'probably deceived' sentence is hedged and not scorable; only the conditional main clause could be scored.

contract.note: The contract rightly requires the antecedent to be shown first. It declines to invent a duration for 'a LONG way away' and does not treat later Level 4 rollouts as settling the claim. Any result would depend on interpretations the speaker did not supply.

evidence.note: A July 2025 CRS report: Level 5 not yet deployed. This fits continued development, but it says nothing about 2023 industry-wide hourly reliance (the antecedent) and cannot measure an undefined 'long way away'.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional forecast whose antecedent, that all self-driving efforts leaned heavily on call centres, is not established by the packet, so it cannot be scored. There is no deadline, and 'a LONG way away' has no duration. The CRS finding that Level 5 had not been deployed is context only. The deception remark is hedged with 'probably'.
